findings.title: Phone users cannot access compile review or ZIP export — fixed desktop columns and clipped header have no narrow-screen alternative
findings.surface: 375px workspace → C++ Snippets / Compile check / UE5 .zip
findings.observed: Layout, theme, visuals and UX: at a 375px viewport the two unshrinkable sidebars exhaust more than the viewport width, leaving the center pane with no usable width, while the header's export controls overflow a clipped application. A phone user cannot use the central compile-check/review flow or ordinarily reach the top-bar ZIP action; no responsive drawer or horizontal recovery scroll is implemented. Source establishes the width conflict; no browser measurement was performed. A desktop is an alternative device, not a recovery on the affected supported phone.
findings.expected: R-210: at 375px "compile-check panel ... primary controls without overlap or clipping ... export actions remain reachable"; checklist, Layout, theme, visuals and UX: "Check containment ... and reachable controls under supported viewports". Fixed sidebars alone require 320+340=660 CSS pixels, exceeding 375 before allocating any center content.
reproduction_steps: Open a saved project in the workspace at 375 CSS pixels wide.
Try to open C++ Snippets and read/run Compile check or AI review.
Try to reach UE5 .zip in the top header.
The fixed 660px of sidebars and non-wrapping header conflict with the overflow-hidden 375px app; no mobile controls replace them.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:647 fixes the left sidebar to w-[320px] shrink-0 and :843 fixes the right to w-[340px] shrink-0, without a narrow-screen replacement. :723 makes the central pane flex-1 min-w-0; its C++ controls live there (:817-824). The header at :587 is a non-wrapping row with all export/save/key buttons (:618-640). frontend/src/App.css:1 fixes the app to 100vw with overflow:hidden; index.css:57-59 also hides document overflow.

findings.title: A substituted Google callback can sign a visitor into someone else's workspace — the new pending flag is not bound to the OAuth transaction
findings.surface: Continue with Google; AuthCallback; POST /api/auth/google
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts login CSRF if a visitor has started (or abandoned) Google sign-in in that tab and then follows a substituted callback carrying another person's valid session id. The boolean admits it without tying it to the initiated sign-in; the server has no corresponding check. The victim can unknowingly generate and save private game-system code in that other account, where its owner can read it. This is conditional on delivering a valid substituted callback while the flag exists; no exploit or provider transaction was executed.
findings.expected: checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: OAuth callbacks 'validate issued state' and 'server-derived authority stays authoritative'. The builder's new browser-started-sign-in safeguard must bind the returned provider session to the actual transaction, not just to any prior click in that tab.
reproduction_steps: In a visitor tab, start Continue with Google, then abandon that sign-in without completing it.
Return in the same tab using a callback link associated with a different valid provider session.
Source predicts that AuthCallback accepts the pending flag and the backend installs the unrelated account session.
A project saved afterwards belongs to that unrelated account.
findings.evidence: Login.jsx:36 writes the constant '1' to sessionStorage and :39 redirects without any app-generated state; AuthPages.jsx:20 only tests that the flag exists and :26 posts the supplied session_id. auth.py:165 accepts only body and response (no browser-bound request/state), :167 retrieves any supplied valid provider session and :189-193 installs it as this browser's session. Projects are saved under the resulting user_id (projects.py:136).

findings.title: Signing out after access-token expiry leaves the refresh session valid — revocation only resolves an unexpired access identity
findings.surface: Account menu > Sign out; POST /api/auth/logout; POST /api/auth/refresh
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: for an email/password user who leaves the workspace idle beyond the 15-minute access lifetime and signs out before another API request refreshes it, logout resolves no user and does not revoke the still-live seven-day refresh token. A retained/copied refresh credential can obtain new access after the user signed out, allowing continued reading and changing private projects. Source proves the expired-access condition bypasses revocation; it does not assert that a credential has actually been stolen.
findings.expected: checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: 'Sign-out ... ends a server-held session' and 'next-request rejection of revoked ... sessions'. The requested sign-out must revoke the refresh authority even when its short-lived access token has expired.
reproduction_steps: Sign in using email/password.
Let the access token expire (15 minutes) without making a protected request; the refresh credential remains valid.
Choose Sign out.
A caller retaining that refresh credential can still call /api/auth/refresh and obtain access because token_version was never incremented.
findings.evidence: auth.py:76-87 optional_user checks access JWTs, Google sessions and bearer tokens, never refresh_token; :58-60 rejects expired access JWTs. logout at :220-221 increments token_version only when optional_user succeeds, otherwise just deletes browser cookies. refresh at :204-212 accepts an existing refresh token with unchanged token_version.

findings.title: Phone users cannot reliably reach AI-key setup or the result — the new flow remains inside a clipped fixed-width desktop workspace

A phone user has no responsive menu or horizontal document scroll to reach the key setup and central result normally. This blocks the essential first-key/synthesis workflow for that cohort; the modal's own max-width is responsive if opened, but does not fix its inaccessible entry point. No browser layout measurement was performed.
findings.expected: R-170: the key window and controls are 'fully visible and usable ... at ... 375px wide'; checklist, Layout, theme, visuals and UX: 'reachable controls under supported viewports'. The new key settings entry point and synthesis result must remain reachable on the supported narrow screen.
reproduction_steps: Open the signed-in workspace at 375px wide.
Try to reach Add AI key in the top bar and then view a synthesis result.
The fixed-width, non-wrapping desktop layout exceeds the viewport while the app/document hide overflow; no small-screen navigation is supplied.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:444 uses a single non-wrapping header with brand, JSON actions, Save, AI-key and account controls; :488 fixes the left sidebar at 320px shrink-0 and :678 fixes the right sidebar at 340px shrink-0. App.css:1 sets width:100vw and overflow:hidden; index.css:57-59 also prevents document scrolling. There is no responsive replacement for these header/sidebar elements.

findings.title: A late save response can cause the next save to overwrite the wrong project — metadata is replaced without checking the active project
findings.surface: Save project while opening another project
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: start saving A, open B before the response, then receive A's save response. The header/role/version become A while the visible result and inputs remain B. A subsequent Save writes B's system into A using A's fresh version, with no conflict warning. This can overwrite another project's valid work with unrelated code under an apparently normal save. Version history may retain the old output, but it does not prevent the wrong-target save and there is no direct restore control. Source predicts consequential cross-project corruption for this reachable slow-save timing.
findings.expected: checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: 'stale work must respect later decisions'; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: preserve object 'identity ... including late client responses'. A response for project A must not relabel project B's open output or redirect its next save to A.
reproduction_steps: Open editable project A and click Save.
Before that request returns, click Open on project B in Projects.
Let A's save finish: A's name reappears while B's system remains displayed.
Click Save: the handler sends B's system to A's project URL.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:298-300 starts a save for the project in the handler closure; :302 unconditionally sets returned metadata as current. ProjectsPanel.jsx:90 leaves project-open buttons enabled while saving; openProject at Workspace.jsx:338-339 changes both metadata and result. splitResult at :289 then reads whichever result is currently shown and the next save at :299 uses whichever metadata the late save installed.

findings.title: Anyone signed in with an invite link can take the invited teammate's access — acceptance never checks the invited email or consumes the token
findings.surface: /invite/:token; POST /api/invites/{token}/accept
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a signed-in recipient of a forwarded or leaked invite link can bind it to a different email, read the team's system and files, and, for an Editor invite, overwrite work. Reusing the link reassigns user_id again, potentially displacing the intended teammate. No owner approval is required; owner removal of the member is the available recovery.
findings.expected: R-076: "is refused when the caller's email differs from the invited address" and "only once"; request: "An invite is sent to an email address." Acceptance must bind only that address and must not let another account replay it.
reproduction_steps: As owner, invite teammate A as Editor and copy the invite link.
Sign in with a different email B and open that link.
The code accepts B and opens the project with Editor access.
Open the same link as another signed-in account; the membership is rebound again.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:226 looks up only members.invite_token; :229-230 sets members.$.user_id to the caller without comparing members.email or marking the invite used. role_for at :33-35 grants the bound user that member's role. frontend/src/pages/AuthPages.jsx:72-75 automatically accepts the token.

findings.title: Two editors can silently overwrite each other's saves — version check is separate from the unconditional update
findings.surface: Save; PUT /api/projects/{id}
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: source predicts that two editors saving from version 1 concurrently can both pass the read-time check before either update. Both writes then succeed (versions 2 and 3), with the latter replacing the former system and inputs, and neither editor receives an overwrite warning. Consequential generated team work is lost without history (Phase 2 is not implemented).
findings.expected: R-068: "you are warned before overwriting"; R-069: an older base_version "returns 409 ... and writes nothing"; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: "conditional/atomic operations" must protect concurrent commit points. Exactly one version-1 save may commit without a warning.
reproduction_steps: Owner and Editor open the same version of a project.
Make different changes in each workspace.
Press Save in both while the requests overlap so both load the old version before either update.
Both return success; reopen and observe that only the later system remains, without a conflict dialog.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:163-168 reads and compares the version, then :169-172 find_one_and_update filters only project_id and increments version. frontend/src/pages/Workspace.jsx:273 sends base_version and :281 shows the warning only on 409.

findings.title: Removed teammates can still fetch their uploaded project files — uploader bypass skips current project permissions
findings.surface: GET /api/files/{file_id}; DELETE /api/files/{file_id}; generation references
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a removed Editor retains authenticated download access to every project file they uploaded even after membership removal or project deletion, and retains delete/use-in-generation access to their references after demotion to Viewer. This defeats the team's revocation boundary; the owner cannot revoke this file access through Share or project deletion.
findings.expected: Request: "Members can upload, download and delete files, according to their role"; R-065: deletion "removes the project and its files"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "Follow ... membership removal ... through every supported access path." Project-linked files must always enforce the current project role and live-project state.
reproduction_steps: As Editor upload a project file and attach a reference; retain their file ids.
As owner remove this Editor in Share (or delete the project).
As the former Editor request download of the uploaded file by its existing file id.
The uploader shortcut still serves it; a reference can also still be deleted or used in generation.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:311-312 returns any file directly to its uploader for a viewer/read check, before :314 load_project. For reference files it also returns directly for editor/delete checks. :187-189 deleting a project only marks the project deleted and never marks files deleted. :341-349 loads references using this same bypass.

findings.title: Opening another project during synthesis can save the first project's output over it — late completion is not tied to its project
findings.surface: Synthesize → Projects → open → Save
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: source predicts a user generating A can open B during the 40–90 second job; A's delayed result then replaces B's displayed system while B's name, role and version stay selected. Pressing Save writes A's code and inputs over B without a conflict because B's version is current. There is no version history to recover B's overwritten system. The running task needs an operation/project identity guard or navigation protection.
findings.expected: Request: projects hold their own "latest generated system" and inputs; checklist, Business logic and calculations: "stale work must respect later decisions"; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: "including late completion after cancel" and context restoration must preserve valid work.
reproduction_steps: Open A and start a regeneration.
Before it finishes, click B's Open row in Projects.
Wait for A's generation to finish; the header still names B but result/context come from A.
Press Save, then reopen B; its previous output has been replaced by A's generation.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:187 awaits generation then :188-191 unconditionally replaces result using the original closure. :305-311 can independently replace project and result while the await runs. ProjectsPanel.jsx:90 open buttons remain enabled while busy (only Stack at :76 uses busy). Workspace.jsx:273 subsequently saves the displayed result to the currently selected project's id.

findings.title: A pre-registered password retains access to the real Google user's projects — account linking trusts an unverified existing email
findings.surface: Email registration → Google account linking → email sign-in
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts someone who pre-registers a teammate's email can keep their chosen password after the real teammate signs in with Google. The real teammate sees a successful Google session and creates private projects in the same user_id; the earlier registrant can log in by password to read or modify those projects and files. No victim password or Google credentials are required for the pre-registration. The victim would need owner-assisted reset to regain sole access.
findings.expected: R-055: "same email address ... one account" must preserve secure identity; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "Establish the actual principals and trust model" and "OAuth ... link/create once". Linking a provider-verified email must not leave an unrelated unverified registrant with ongoing access.
reproduction_steps: Register an email/password account using another person's email (without email verification).
Have the actual email owner sign in through Google with that address and save a private project.
Sign in with the password chosen during pre-registration.
That session has the same user_id and can access the real owner's newly saved work.
findings.evidence: auth.py:127-134 permits registering an unverified email with a password. :168-171 merges a subsequent Google sign-in into that row and sets email_verified True, without removing or re-proving its existing password. :147-156 continues accepting that password. Project ownership is keyed by user_id (projects.py:31).

findings.title: Signing out does not revoke email sessions — access and refresh JWTs have no server-side session or revocation check
findings.surface: Sign out; POST /api/auth/logout and /refresh; authenticated APIs
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a retained email access token can continue reading and writing private projects for its remaining 15 minutes after Sign out; a retained refresh credential can mint further access for seven days. Clearing the UI cookies does not invalidate a captured session. Signing out therefore cannot terminate a compromised/shared email session; Google sessions do have a database deletion path.
findings.expected: Request: "sign-out"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "next-request rejection of revoked/deleted sessions" and "Sign-out ... ends a server-held session." A signed-out email session must not remain usable with its old credentials.
reproduction_steps: Sign in with email/password and retain that session's credentials in an authorized API client.
Use Account menu → Sign out.
Reuse the old access credential for GET /api/projects; it remains accepted until expiry.
Reuse the old refresh credential for POST /api/auth/refresh; it can still renew access.
findings.evidence: auth.py:32 JWT payload has sub/type/exp but no session identity; :55-62 validates signature and user existence only. Logout :207-210 deletes only Google session rows and client cookies. Refresh :196-201 accepts the previous signed refresh token without a revoked-session lookup.

findings.title: Unsolicited Google callbacks can log a visitor into another account — callback exchange lacks browser-bound state validation
findings.surface: Google sign-in callback
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts an unsolicited callback URL containing a valid broker session identifier for a different account is exchanged and sets that account's session cookie, without proof that this browser initiated that login. A signed-out visitor can be logged into another person's account and unknowingly save private UE5 work there. Broker-side validity proves the identifier's identity, not this browser's intent; actual broker issuance behavior was not executed.
findings.expected: R-054: "checks the OAuth state value issued at sign-in start ... a callback whose state value does not match is refused"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "validate issued state." An uninitiated callback must not change the browser's signed-in identity.
reproduction_steps: Obtain a valid broker callback identifier for account A in a controlled authentication flow.
In a different signed-out browser that never started Google login, open the app callback location carrying that identifier.
The frontend posts it and the backend sets account A's cookie without checking browser-bound state.
Saving work would then store it under A.
findings.evidence: Login.jsx:35-38 starts broker auth with redirect only, with no app nonce. App.js:21 accepts any session_id fragment. AuthPages.jsx:18-19 exchanges it immediately. auth.py:161-163 receives only session_id and verifies it with the provider but never binds it to a browser-initiated state.

findings.title: Regeneration and stacking cannot preserve existing implementation — both discard source, pseudocode, graph and most code before calling Claude
findings.surface: Regenerate and Stack Systems model context
findings.observed: AI and model features: source proves custom behavior contained only in the previous .cpp, pseudocode, setup, graph or the omitted header tail is never sent on regeneration or stacking. For example, a saved damage system with a bespoke combo-reset rule only in its .cpp cannot have that rule preserved from the provided context when the user only changes Max Health, nor can stacking inspect its implementation conflicts. The model receives a summary, not the previous output. Output quality itself was not sampled; omitted context is deterministic and forces users to re-supply implementation manually.
findings.expected: R-087: previous output is sent with explicit revision instructions; request: "regeneration should visibly respect the edits" and stack should "combine them into a single synthesized output ... avoids conflicts." Unchanged implementation and cross-system logic must be available to the model for a faithful revision/merge.
reproduction_steps: Open a saved system whose .cpp contains an implementation detail not in its header or summary.
Change only a parameter and Synthesize, or select it with another project and Stack.
Trace compactForApi and build_user_text: the complete source, pseudocode and graph are absent from the model input.
The model cannot faithfully revise/merge that omitted implementation.
findings.evidence: changes.js:75-83 compactForApi sends only name/summary/modules/params/network notes and the first 2500 header characters; it drops cpp_source, pseudocode, graph and setup. Workspace.jsx:220 and :238 use it for regeneration and stacking. server.py:211-222 compacts again and :236 limits stacked headers to 1800 characters. :185-186 promises preserving unaffected content and integrating systems.

findings.title: Phone users cannot reach generated output and tuning actions — desktop-only fixed panels exceed a viewport with hidden overflow
findings.surface: Workspace and public share view at 375px width
findings.observed: Layout, theme, visuals and UX: source predicts that at 375px the two fixed sidebars alone require 660px, exceeding the viewport by 285px before any center content. The right dials and generated output are clipped with no outer scrolling, and full-text public header/tab buttons overflow as well. A phone user cannot complete tuning/viewing/copying through the intended workspace. This is a source layout deduction, not a browser measurement.
findings.expected: R-117: primary content and Synthesize/Copy JSON are usable "at 1440px and at 375px wide"; checklist, Layout, theme, visuals and UX: "containment ... scrolling and reachable controls under supported viewports." At narrow widths core output and actions must remain accessible.
reproduction_steps: Open the signed-in workspace at 375px CSS width.
Generate a system and try to view the central tabs and tune the right panel.
Open a public share link at the same width and try its Copy JSON and tab actions.
Fixed rows exceed the clipped viewport with no responsive navigation.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:426 fixes left sidebar to w-[320px] shrink-0 and :606 fixes right sidebar to w-[340px] shrink-0 in a single flex row (:423), with main min-w-0 (:502). The header (:385-419) has unwrapped branding/actions. PublicView.jsx:35-51 also uses unwrapped full-text header/tab actions. index.css:57-59 and App.css:1 hide outer overflow; there is no responsive sidebar alternative.

findings.title: Exporters receive empty C++ and setup files as a successful ZIP — builders never validate required content
findings.surface: Workspace → UE5 .zip → either option; Export anyway
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: source predicts that a developer importing a legacy/partial system with a name but missing C++ or setup can export an empty, unusable archive. Missing setup alone is not even flagged by checkSystem, which only checks C++. The new catch cannot help because neither builder throws for missing content. The user must inspect the archive and regenerate missing sections; the project itself remains unchanged.
findings.expected: R-217: "If a project's stored C++ or setup content is missing ... shows an error naming the missing part and downloads no partial zip"; R-201 requires an explanation rather than empty files. Missing-content validation should precede packaging, independently of the permission to export compilable-content warnings.
reproduction_steps: Import project JSON containing a named system with missing cpp_source, or a C++ pair but no setup_guide.
Open UE5 .zip and choose Unreal plugin or Source files only.
If prompted, press Export anyway.
Inspect the predicted archive: the absent section is empty/a heading, despite the success toast.
findings.evidence: frontend/src/lib/zipExport.js:113-114 writes cpp_header || "" and cpp_source || ""; :68-74 renders even an absent setup_guide as a heading; :174-175 does the same for plugin modules. frontend/src/pages/Workspace.jsx:438 only checks result existence, :440 allows issues to be bypassed, :446 builds and :453-454 announces a successful no-code-edits download. backend/projects.py:139-141 accepts an imported system with only system_name.

findings.title: AI review can report a malformed answer as clean — invalid issue entries are silently discarded
findings.surface: POST /api/ai/review-cpp; C++ Snippets → AI review
findings.observed: AI and model features: when the provider returns a list containing malformed issue records, the endpoint converts an unreadable review into a successful empty review. A developer is incorrectly reassured the review found no additional problems and can export without those warnings. Actual provider output was not executed; this is the exact source-predicted consequence for those responses. Retrying the review is possible but the UI gives no reason to do so.
findings.expected: R-194 requires returned issues, a clean message when none are found, or an error; checklist, AI and model features: "Follow parsing, semantic validation ... against the ... field/format ... contract." Malformed issues are not evidence of clean code and must surface a readable-review error rather than a clean verdict.
reproduction_steps: Press AI review on a C++ pair.
Consider a provider response whose JSON issues array contains a string issue, or an object missing message.
Trace review_cpp: each entry is filtered out and HTTP success returns an empty list.
The panel displays No further problems found and export has no AI issue warning.
findings.evidence: backend/server.py:482-484 validates only that issues is a list; :485-491 filters out all non-dicts and entries lacking a truthy message. Thus {"issues":["missing implementation"]} or {"issues":[{"file":".cpp"}]} becomes {issues:[]}. frontend/src/components/CompileCheck.jsx:80 displays "No further problems found." for that response; Workspace.jsx:571 also receives no AI export warnings.

findings.title: Plugin exports using WidgetLayoutLibrary fail to build without edits — dependency detection omits its UMG module
findings.surface: UE5 .zip → Unreal plugin; Bundle plugin → Download
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: a valid stored system that includes Blueprint/WidgetLayoutLibrary.h and calls UWidgetLayoutLibrary::GetViewportScale, with no other UMG-matching symbols, exports with only Core/CoreUObject/Engine dependencies. WidgetLayoutLibrary belongs to UMG, so this otherwise valid UI system cannot compile/link as the advertised drop-in plugin until a developer edits Build.cs. The same failure affects a selected bundle module. This is a source prediction; Unreal compilation was not run.
findings.expected: request: "ready-made Unreal plugin ... so it installs with no code edits"; R-208: "module list ... exactly the set of engine modules the generated code requires, detected from the code's includes and macros". For this witness the independent dependency is UMG, the module that provides Blueprint/WidgetLayoutLibrary.h, regardless of whether code also happens to use UUserWidget.
reproduction_steps: Open/import a system whose valid C++ includes Blueprint/WidgetLayoutLibrary.h and calls UWidgetLayoutLibrary::GetViewportScale, without UUserWidget, UMG or WidgetComponent text.
Export Unreal plugin, or include it alongside another system in Bundle plugin.
Inspect that module's Build.cs: UMG is absent.
Attempt the promised install in a UE5 project without adding dependencies manually; the exported module lacks its required UMG dependency.
findings.evidence: frontend/src/lib/zipExport.js:26 recognizes UMG only via /UUserWidget|UMG|WidgetComponent/; the entire DEPS list (:24-38) has no WidgetLayoutLibrary match. :168-172 writes only matched modules plus sibling deps into Build.cs; :174-175 copies the code. Bundle exports use that same writeModule at :260.

findings.title: Older saved versions disappear from Compare and history after 1,000 saves — version listing silently truncates without pagination
findings.surface: Compare → Compare against / History / Restore
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: after version 1001 is saved, v1 (and its label/note) is absent from all history and Compare menus even though its snapshot is still stored. An owner/editor cannot discover or restore an important earliest version through the app; viewers also lose its history. Directly constructing a version API request is not an ordinary UI recovery. Source predicts truncation; no thousand-save runtime test was performed.
findings.expected: R-156: "lists every snapshot newest first"; R-190: "history listing every saved version with its note, saver and time"; request: "roll a project back to any saved version from the Compare menu". Pagination or another reachable continuation must expose the oldest snapshots as well.
reproduction_steps: Use a project that has 1001 saved snapshots, naming v1 as an important checkpoint.
Open Compare and History.
Search the named and all-versions groups for v1: the API returns only v1001 through v2.
There is no next-page/load-more control to access or restore v1.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:214-216 sorts all snapshots by version descending then calls to_list(1000), returning no total/cursor at :217-219. frontend/src/pages/Workspace.jsx:488-489 sets versions to only this reply; :532-533 and frontend/src/components/HistoryModal.jsx:9 list only these versions; restore controls require choosing one (:495-508).

findings.title: A restored version can lose its provenance note during a concurrent save — backfill wins the snapshot race and restore swallows the duplicate
findings.surface: Compare → Restore vN; concurrent project Save; Version history
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: let restore change v2 to v3, then let another editor save before restore's snapshot insert. The save backfills v3 with an empty note and creates v4. Restore's v3 insert then hits the unique index and is silently ignored. The restored contents survive, but the promised 'Restored from vN' history note is permanently lost, leaving the team without the restore's explanation. Ordinary sequential restores work; this finding is the evidenced concurrent interleaving, not a runtime observation.
findings.expected: R-177: a restore creates a newest version "whose note reads 'Restored from vN'"; R-190 requires the restored version's note in history. The note and snapshot must describe the same committed restore even when a collaborator immediately saves afterward.
reproduction_steps: As an editor, restore v1 of a v2 project.
Before restore inserts the v3 snapshot, have a second editor load v3 and save it as v4.
The second save backfills v3 without a note.
Allow restore's snapshot insert to finish: it fails as a duplicate and is ignored; History shows v3 without Restored from v1.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:241-249 updates the project to the restored version before inserting its snapshot with 'Restored from vN'; :250-251 swallows snapshot failure. A concurrent save reads that new project and :185-189 backfills its missing snapshot with snapshot(project), whose default note is empty (:66-70). Reload to obtain the correct zero.

findings.title: Keyboard focus escapes the new dialogs and leaves background actions active — shared Modal has no focus management
findings.surface: New bundle, history, save, limit-warning and export-check dialogs via shared Modal
findings.observed: Layout, theme, visuals and UX: keyboard users opening Bundle plugin, History, or export warnings keep focus on the triggering background control. Tab traverses the workspace rather than entering a confined dialog, and can leave even the Save dialog after its last control. Background actions remain operable under the visual backdrop, making accidental project changes and finding the actual confirmation controls possible only through a long traversal. Escape remains a safe close path; this is a meaningful accessibility impairment, not a measured visual issue.

findings.title: Bundles omit dependencies used only through sibling headers or delegates — dependency planning matches class names rather than includes
findings.surface: Projects → Bundle plugin → sibling module dependency planning
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: suppose Health's header declares UHealthComponent and FOnHealthChanged via a delegate macro, and Stamina includes HealthComponent.h but uses only FOnHealthChanged. The bundler never recognizes that as using HealthKit, so StaminaKit.Build.cs lacks HealthKit and Unreal cannot resolve the sibling public header on its module include path. Bundling valid interoperating systems therefore requires manual Build.cs edits. This is a source-predicted dependency omission; no exported plugin was compiled.
findings.expected: R-187: "copying the folder ... installs every selected system together"; R-208: required engine dependencies and request: "with its own module files, so it installs with no code edits"; checklist, Files, media and generated artifacts: trace structure and dependencies through to usable output. A consumer that includes a sibling module's public header needs that sibling in Build.cs, even if it uses only a delegate declared there.
reproduction_steps: Have a Health project with HealthComponent.generated.h, UHealthComponent and a macro-declared FOnHealthChanged delegate.
Have a Stamina project whose code includes HealthComponent.h and uses FOnHealthChanged without referencing UHealthComponent.
Bundle both projects and inspect StaminaKit.Build.cs.
HealthKit is absent; add it manually to make the sibling public include available.
findings.evidence: zipExport.js:13-15 extracts only class/struct identifiers; :225 adds sibling dependencies only when such an identifier appears in the consumer code. It does not inspect sibling #include paths or DECLARE_*DELEGATE names. :254 passes only p.uses to writeModule, which writes those dependencies at :164-167.

findings.title: A successful concurrent save can report failure — backfill and post-save snapshot inserts race on the same version
findings.surface: Save project; PUT /api/projects/{project_id}; version history
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: source-predicted interleaving: A commits v2 and pauses before line 195; B loads v2, finds its snapshot missing and backfills v2 at line 180; A's line 195 now raises duplicate-key and returns 500 although A's content is already saved. A sees 'Couldn't save', retains the stale base version and must reopen or resolve a spurious conflict. This affects simultaneous team saves and miscommunicates a committed operation; the atomic project update itself prevents silent content overwriting.
findings.expected: R-156: 'Every project create and every successful save writes an immutable snapshot'; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: 'Identify commit points ... inspect ... completion recording ... and communicated uncertainty.' Saving and recording a version must not race into reporting a committed save as rejected.
reproduction_steps: Open the same project in two editor sessions.
Have editor A save v1 to v2; before its snapshot insert completes, let editor B load v2 and save.
B backfills the missing v2 snapshot; A's unconditional v2 insert violates the unique index.
A receives 'Couldn't save' even though its v2 write committed.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:178-182 checks for a missing current snapshot and inserts it, swallowing exceptions; :184-188 atomically updates the project/version; :195 then unconditionally inserts that new version snapshot. server.py:54 declares (project_id, version) unique. Workspace.jsx:307-308 treats a non-409 error as 'Couldn't save' and leaves its old version metadata.

findings.title: Long-lived projects lose access to older comparisons — version lists silently stop at 1,000 snapshots
findings.surface: Compare base selector; GET /api/projects/{id}/versions
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: after a team makes 1,001 saved versions, v1 is still stored but is absent from the only version list and Compare selector. More saves push further earlier versions out. The user cannot select those versions through the app; there is no pagination or truncation notice. This is a bounded history-access failure, recoverable only through a caller knowing the omitted version number, not through the UI.
findings.expected: request: 'Keep every saved version of a project so Compare works against any earlier one, not just the last'; R-156: 'lists every snapshot newest first'; R-157: 'every saved version of the open project'. All retained versions must be reachable, with pagination if needed.
reproduction_steps: Accumulate 1,001 saves on a project.
Reopen it and open Compare.
Open 'Compare against': only v1001 through v2 are returned; v1 is unavailable.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:203-205 sorts versions descending and calls '.to_list(1000)' without an offset, cursor or total; Workspace.jsx:388 uses that single response and :408-411 renders only those returned versions.

findings.title: Paid users with exhausted credits are told their model requires a paid key — all insufficient-quota errors are classified as free-tier refusals
findings.surface: AI key window Test key/Save; synthesis error banner
findings.observed: Third-party integrations: for an OpenAI account that already has a paid key but has exhausted its balance or spending quota, the provider's insufficient_quota response is converted into a false free-tier diagnosis. Settings blocks saving that model and offers Gemini instead of explaining credit/quota recovery. Users lose the correct cause and perform needless key/model changes; no unauthorized billing or actual provider response was observed.

Select GPT-4.1 and press Test key.
When the provider reports insufficient_quota, the app says the key is free-tier and blocks saving with a paid-key error.

findings.title: Stacking discards the saved implementations before asking the AI to merge — only metadata and a header excerpt reach the provider
findings.surface: Projects > Stack N systems
findings.observed: AI and model features: choose two saved projects whose summaries/headers are similar but whose .cpp contains distinct game logic. Neither implementation is sent to the selected provider. The merge cannot ground its result in either actual implementation and may replace existing behavior with invented logic. This is a source-proven omission, not an assertion about a specific unexecuted model reply. Users can still generate a new combined architecture, but cannot rely on Stack to build on their saved code.
findings.expected: request: 'Stack Systems ... keep working with cloud projects' and teams 'build on the same systems'; R-155 calls for 'one merged system'; checklist, AI and model features: 'Compare the promised task with the actual ... source records ... transformations, truncation ... that could remove essential meaning.' Select both in Projects and click Stack 2 systems.
Trace the posted stack_systems and provider prompt: neither contains cpp_source or the setup/pseudocode bodies.

findings.title: Regenerating a longer saved system loses the tail of its code context — the backend still truncates the supposedly full previous implementation
findings.surface: Synthesize / Regenerate with N changes
findings.observed: AI and model features: a valid saved/imported project with a .cpp longer than 12,000 characters can be reopened and regenerated, but code after that boundary never reaches the model. This predicts omitted revision context rather than claiming a particular generated code loss was executed; users must manually reconcile long implementations.
findings.expected: request: teams should 'build on the same systems'; R-169 requires previous inputs map into the complete system; checklist, AI and model features: inspect 'transformations, truncation ... that could remove essential meaning'. The exposed revision contract at server.py:192 is 'Keep everything ... not affected'; the full implementation must reach that revision or the user must be warned/refused before it is silently omitted.
reproduction_steps: Import/open a valid project with a cpp_source over 12,000 characters and a meaningful function at the end.
Queue a dial or parameter change and regenerate.
Inspect the source path: only cpp_source[:12000] is used in the provider prompt, despite the full previous_system sent by the browser.

SYSTEM_PROMPT at :192 promises to keep everything unaffected.

findings.title: Linking a normal email account to Google disables its existing email sign-in — every unverified password is deleted without a replacement flow

Sign out, then Continue with Google using that email.
Sign out and try the original email/password.
It is rejected; signup with the same email is also refused, leaving Google or an owner-issued reset as the only recovery.

findings.title: Keyboard focus stays in the covered workspace when key settings opens — the dialog lacks focus management and trapping

findings.title: Partial model results are reported as complete systems — validation permits empty sections and blank setup instructions

The job is stored as done and the partial system is displayed instead of an incomplete-output failure.

findings.title: Compare can show another project's baseline after switching — version fetches apply stale responses without an identity check
findings.surface: Compare > Compare against; switching projects during a version fetch

It installs A's baseline after the B-change reset; Compare now shows A's code as 'v1' against B and can offer B's version selector with that same number selected. Out-of-order selections within one project can likewise revert the user's latest choice. The user receives a misleading comparison and must reselect the version to recover; both projects are authorized, so this is not a data-access claim.
findings.expected: R-157: choosing a version 'diffs that version against the current system'; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: follow identifiers and 'context restoration ... alternate entry points' and ignore stale work after later decisions. The selected baseline must belong to the currently open project and latest selection.
reproduction_steps: Open project A > Compare and choose a saved version while the request is slow.
Open B before the version-detail response arrives.
Allow A's response to finish, then open Compare on B.
A's version is used as the baseline for B until a new selection replaces it.

findings.title: Returning to a project lets an obsolete regeneration replace its newly loaded version — the discard guard checks id but not editing lifecycle
findings.surface: Regenerate while switching away from and back to a project
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: start regenerating A v1, open B, then reopen A after another editor saved v2. When the original generation completes, the id comparison passes and it replaces v2 in the workspace with a revision based on v1; project metadata still holds v2, so saving that output does not trigger the overwrite warning. Users can silently reintroduce stale content despite the new discard guard. Saved history mitigates recovery, but the newly loaded collaborative state is not preserved.
findings.expected: checklist, Business logic and calculations: 'stale work must respect later decisions'; request: teammates must not 'silently undo each other's work'. A revision started on A v1 must not replace a subsequently loaded A v2 merely because its project id is equal.
reproduction_steps: Start a regeneration on project A at v1.
Switch to B while it runs.
Have another editor save A v2, then reopen A in the first workspace.
Let the v1 generation finish: it is applied to the now-v2 workspace and can be saved without a conflict.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:203 records only project_id and :209 compares only the final project_id. openProject at :336-339 can reload the same project at a newer version while a synthesis runs; :213-214 then installs the older closure's result/context if the final id equals the original, regardless of intervening switches/reloads.

findings.title: Accepted PDF references can be invisible to the AI — only truncated extracted text is sent, never scanned pages
findings.surface: Attach reference > PDF > Synthesize
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: attach a scanned/image-only specification PDF. Upload succeeds and its chip is retained, but extract_text yields no content and no PDF page image or PDF bytes are sent to the AI. The reference in the prompt contains only its filename. Text-bearing content after page 40 or 20,000 characters is also silently omitted. The user believes the PDF grounded the synthesis but must manually convert/select its content to recover. This is source-predicted omission, not an executed judgment about model output.
findings.expected: request: 'Accepted types are screenshots and images, PDFs, and code or text files' and 'The AI uses them as source material'; R-169: 'attached references ... in the shape that provider expects'; checklist, Files, media and generated artifacts: compare 'complete intended content and actual input selection'. Image-only PDF pages must reach the model or be rejected/explained instead of silently accepted as empty source.
reproduction_steps: Attach a PDF containing a scanned UI specification with no text layer.
Ask Synthesize to match the PDF's design.
Follow the reference path: its extracted text is empty and it is not added to image attachments.
The provider receives the filename but none of the scanned design.
findings.evidence: projects.py:306-307 extracts text from only the first 40 PDF pages and truncates to TEXT_CHARS=20000 (:23); upload stores that text at :347. load_references at :394-396 sends image bytes only when content_type starts with image/, not for PDFs. server.py:242 selects '(image attached below)' only for image_bytes, otherwise text or ''; :244 sends this as source material.

findings.title: Some 503 responses fail without the promised retries — overload detection matches text formatting rather than the HTTP status
findings.surface: Gemini synthesis busy-response handling
findings.observed: Third-party integrations: a Gemini 503 exception with numeric status 503 but the quoted UNAVAILABLE/single-quoted error representation is not classified busy, so the first request fails immediately with generic provider text rather than receiving the two retries and busy explanation. Users facing transient overload lose an otherwise recoverable generation attempt and must retry manually. This is a conditional source trace for that exception shape, not an observed provider outage.
findings.expected: R-106: 'a 503 is retried twice before failing'; R-168: 'When Gemini returns 503 ... retries the same request twice ... reports a busy error'. Status-code identity is 503 regardless of capitalization, JSON versus Python-repr quotes or provider wording; use structured status/code information or cover that supported error shape.
reproduction_steps: Run a Gemini synthesis when the provider returns HTTP 503 with an UNAVAILABLE exception whose message is 'The service is currently unavailable' and whose error dict is rendered with single quotes.
The busy matcher sees neither its hardcoded words nor double-quoted code fragment.
The job fails after one attempt instead of three.
findings.evidence: classify_error at server.py:282 recognizes busy only through a few string fragments, including double-quoted '"code": 503', and never inspects an exception's status_code. :321 retries only if this classifier returns busy. A 503 exception rendered as "503 UNAVAILABLE. {'error': {'code': 503, 'message': 'The service is currently unavailable'}}" matches none of the fragments and falls through to generic 'error' at :284.

findings.title: A provider timeout produces an empty-cause error banner — synthesis error classification omits timeouts
findings.surface: Synthesis Failed banner; GET /api/generate/{job_id}
findings.observed: Third-party integrations: if generation's awaited provider call raises TimeoutError, run_job does end the job and preserves the previous project, but the user gets only 'AI provider error: ' and code='error'. The timeout cause is lost even though the key-test path knows how to explain it. Users cannot tell whether to fix their key, change input or retry. This is bounded error-recovery impairment; no timeout was induced.
findings.expected: R-105: failure 'shows a message in plain English naming that cause'; R-106 explicitly includes 'provider timeout' and machine-readable error_code; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: resolve failure with 'visible feedback and promised recovery'. A provider timeout must be identified as a timeout with usable retry guidance.
reproduction_steps: Start a generation whose provider request raises TimeoutError.
Poll the generation job.
The job is error with generic code and an empty-cause 'AI provider error: ' banner rather than a timeout message.
findings.evidence: server.py:287-296 handles authentication/quota/model-unavailable substrings but has no timeout branch; an asyncio.TimeoutError has an empty str and returns 'AI provider error: '. run_job at :336-337 persists code='error' and that detail. test_key has its own explicit timeout explanation at :407-408, but generate does not.

findings.title: Other open tabs keep using a removed or replaced key — key settings are read only when the workspace mounts
findings.surface: AI key Remove/Save across two open workspace tabs

A user rotating/removing a credential can unintentionally continue consuming that old key's quota or paid usage. This is limited to already mounted tabs; a newly opened or reloaded tab reads the correct saved setting.

[the no-key prompt] and no job starts', and 'after replacement the next synthesis uses the new key and model'; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: 'Settings persist and affect the promised behaviour throughout the app.' Browser-local rotation/removal must take effect in already open tabs too, or the UI must explicitly limit the claim to the current tab.

In the first tab, Remove the key or replace it with B and save.
Without reloading, synthesize in the second tab.
Its request still carries A, and removal did not return it to the add-key prompt.

Workspace.jsx:164 calls loadAiKey only as the initial useState initializer; its subsequent generate at :198 checks that in-memory value and :208 forwards it. No storage event subscription or per-generation reload exists in these paths.

findings.title: Email/password invitees do not see invited projects on sign-in — automatic access is limited to Google-verified accounts
findings.surface: Projects → Shared with me; email sign-in

As owner add that email as Viewer or Editor in Share.
Sign in as that teammate without opening the invite link.
Open Shared with me: the query excludes the pending membership.

findings.title: Reopened projects use another project's bias and omit saved notes — openSystem never restores these inputs
findings.surface: Projects → open; Project Context and Notes for next synthesis

Saved context exists in Mongo but is ignored, so teammates and cross-device users must reconstruct it manually and can generate the wrong architecture.

reproduction_steps: Generate and save A with one Project Context preset and designer notes.
Change the browser's context to a different preset while working on B.
Open A from Projects.
A's saved context and notes are not restored; Synthesize sends the other preset.
